title: Anderson localization on the Bethe lattice
authors: Dafne Prado Bandeira, Angelica Vecchiarelli, Marco Tarzia
abstract: Anderson localization is a paradigmatic disorder-driven quantum phase transition in which interference effects can completely suppress wave propagation. Its formulation on the Bethe lattice -- an infinite tree with fixed coordination number -- provides a unique setting in which the transition becomes analytically tractable. Owing to its exponential volume growth, the Bethe lattice realizes the infinite-dimensional limit of the Anderson problem and also serves as a useful mean-field-like description of localization in many-body configuration spaces.   These lecture notes provide a pedagogical review of Anderson localization on the Bethe lattice, focusing on the resolvent (Green's function) formalism and the cavity approach. We discuss the main diagnostics of localization and show how they are encoded in the statistical properties of Green's functions, with the full probability distribution of the local density of states emerging as the natural order parameter of the transition. We derive the cavity self-consistent equations for the diagonal resolvent and review both their numerical solution by population dynamics and their analytical treatment in the large-connectivity limit. This framework gives access to the critical disorder and the critical behavior near the transition, including the localization length in the insulating phase and the correlation volume that controls the delocalized phase. We also discuss the connection with directed polymers in random media and its interpretation in terms of rare resonant paths and freezing phenomena.   These notes originated from a series of lectures delivered by one of the authors at the Oropa Summer School on "Fundamental Problems in Statistical Physics XVI" (July 2025).
summary: This work provides a comprehensive, pedagogical review of Anderson localization theory by focusing on the exactly solvable Bethe lattice model. It details how disorder drives a true quantum phase transition, characterizing it using advanced Green's function techniques and self-consistent equations. The paper is crucial for understanding the theoretical limits of wave propagation in disordered media.
main_problem: The paper investigates Anderson localization, a quantum phase transition where disorder suppresses wave propagation, by analyzing its behavior on the Bethe lattice.
main_result: It establishes that the Bethe lattice provides an analytically tractable framework to study this transition, revealing diagnostics like spectral statistics and the divergence of correlation volumes at criticality.
method: The analysis relies heavily on the resolvent (Green's function) formalism and the cavity approach to derive self-consistent equations for the system's properties.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Anderson Hamiltonian applied to the Bethe lattice, which serves as an infinite-dimensional limit of disordered quantum systems. It also draws analogies to Many-Body Localization (MBL).
key_observables: Localization length ($\xi$), full probability distribution of the local density of states, Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR), and the crossing of $\langle \ln Z angle$ through zero.
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($W$) relative to hopping amplitude ($t$), connectivity/coordination number, and system dimension (comparing finite $d$ vs. infinite Bethe limit).
main_assumptions: The use of the Bethe lattice assumes an infinite-dimensional, tree-like structure, which simplifies calculations but neglects loop correlations present in real lattices.
figures_summary: Not specified; the notes refer to general concepts like schematic representations of configuration spaces (e.g., hypercubes).
paper_structure: The review progresses from defining Anderson localization and its diagnostics (Green's functions, IPR) to detailing the mathematical machinery (resolvent/cavity approach) used on the Bethe lattice, culminating in discussions about critical behavior and connections to DPRM.
why_interesting: The rigorous analytical treatment of a quantum phase transition using advanced Green's function techniques is highly relevant for understanding localization phenomena in open or disordered quantum systems studied in AMO physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic representation of the configuration space of the spin chain (Eq. (21)) for L = 3 in the basis of the simultaneous eigenstates of the {σz i } operators. Each vertex corresponds to one of the 23 = 8 spin configurations. To each vertex, a random energy is assigned (indicated by color) containing linear combinations of the random fields hi, weighted by the spin values of that specific configuration. Edges connect configurations that differ by a single spin flip, forming a 3-dimensional hypercube structure.

Figure 2. (Left) For a finite system, G(z) is analytic except at a discrete set of points on the real axis corresponding to the eigenvalues λn, where it exhibits simple poles. (Right) In the thermodynamic limit (N →∞), these discrete poles may merge into a continuous branch cut along the real axis. The physical Green’s functions are recovered by approaching the real axis from the complex plane through the regularization z = λ ± iη (green dots) as η →0+.

Figure 3. Energy spectrum of the system in the extended phase. Each horizontal line represents an eigenstate at energy λn, with its oscillatory pattern indicating the spatial structure. The red marker shows that the amplitude of the wavefunction is uniformly of order O(1/N).

Figure 4. Integrated local density of states Ri(E) in the extended phase. Both the step height (proportional to |ψn(i)|2) and the level spacing are of order O(1/N). In the thermodynamic limit, these discrete steps merge into a smooth, continuous function.

Figure 5. Energy spectrum in the localized regime. Each eigenstate is confined to a region around its localization center. At site i, the local density of states receives significant contributions only from eigenstates whose centers lie within ∼ξ of i; distant states contribute negligibly.
